EverYield Bond: Questions Surrounding Placement and Trading – Criminal Complaint Filed in Connection with the Bond
Schirp Schmidt-Morsbach Rechtsanwälte Investigate Civil Claims for Damages and Call on Investors to Come Forward

Berlin, 24 November 2026 – The law firm Schirp Schmidt-Morsbach Rechtsanwälte PartG mbB is investigating potential civil claims for damages in connection with the EverYield bond. According to financial journalist Christian Schiffmacher, he has filed a criminal complaint concerning suspected market manipulation and fraud. At the centre of the matter are bonds with a nominal value of EUR 40 million which, according to the prospectus supplement, reportedly generated no cash inflow for the issuer, and the question of whether these bonds were subsequently sold to external investors.
Dr. Schirp, attorney-at-law, states: “In our view, the documents available to us to date raise substantial questions regarding the economic basis, placement and use of the bond.”
The following chronology is based on our analysis to date of the documents available to us:

June and July 2026: Increase in bond issue volume and reported placement success: On 15 June 2026, EverYield increased the initially announced issue volume from EUR 30 million to EUR 50 million, citing “strong investor interest and significantly expanded financing prospects”. The bond was marketed directly by the issuer without the involvement of a placing bank. On 1 July, EverYield announced the successful completion of the placement, with a total placement volume of EUR 41 million.

July to September: Commencement of exchange trading and dramatic price decline: Trading commenced on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange’s Open Market on 8 July. On 20 July, EverYield announced plans for a research and innovation centre in Stuttgart. Despite this positive announcement, the bond price plummeted. By 7 August, the closing price had already fallen to just 19.95 per cent of its nominal value.

On 10 August, management stated that the price movements had no impact on, and were unrelated to, the company’s strategic direction or operational business activities. By early September, the bond, which had been marketed as secured, was trading at below 10 per cent of its nominal value.

October: Questions surrounding the subscription of bonds worth EUR 40 million: On 2 October, the closing price of the bond had fallen to just 0.5 per cent of its nominal value. On 5 October, the issuer published a prospectus supplement stating that an unnamed “platform provider” had subscribed for bonds worth EUR 40 million without generating any cash inflow for EverYield.

According to the prospectus supplement, payment of the subscription price had been deferred until 1 July 2032 and was to be offset against licence fee claims arising under the “Master Platform License Agreement”.

By the time the prospectus supplement was published on 5 October, including trading on that date, bonds with an aggregate nominal value of more than EUR 24.6 million had already been traded on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange.

“EUR 40 million in bond subscriptions without any fresh funds flowing into the company: investors need to know what was behind the reported placement success, what projects actually existed and which projects were intended to be financed,” explains Dr. Wolfgang Schirp, an attorney-at-law based in Berlin.

On 29 October, the German consumer protection organisation Stiftung Warentest reported that the EUR 10 million pledged by the sole shareholder, Mildner Immo Besitz GmbH, had not yet been contributed to the company.

EverYield CEO Mario Mildner stated that the shareholder was covering ongoing expenses and that further funding was tied to milestones in the development of the company. Regarding the late publication of the prospectus supplement, he explained that legal advisers had recommended its publication as early as 24 July, followed by a coordination and approval process.

November: Trading volume exceeding EUR 27.8 million and criminal complaint: Exchange trading in the bond continued. By 17 November, bonds with an aggregate nominal value of more than EUR 27.8 million had been traded on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange alone.

These trading volumes raise questions as to which securities accounts the bonds traded originated from. In his report, Schiffmacher states that internal documents provided to him anonymously contain information concerning a platform provider. The origin of the bonds traded and the underlying transactions require further investigation.

“The key evidence now lies in the subscription records, securities account records and transaction documents: Who received the bonds, who sold them, and where did the proceeds go? We are investigating potential claims with the aim of securing compensation for investors who have suffered losses,” says Dr. Wolfgang Schirp.
The issues outlined above require further clarification.

Investors are encouraged to come forward: The law firm calls on both initial subscribers and investors who subsequently purchased the bonds on the stock exchange to come forward, including those who have already sold their bonds at a loss.

In particular, the firm is seeking purchase and sale confirmations, securities account statements, subscription documents, marketing materials and correspondence with intermediaries or advisers. Information concerning sellers may also help to reconstruct the chain of transactions involving the bonds.
Contact and information for investors: Dr. Wolfgang Schirp, Schirp Schmidt-Morsbach Rechtsanwälte PartG mbB, Kantstraße 149, 10623 Berlin, Germany, Email: schirp@schirp.com, Tel.: +49 179 5320213
Note to editors:** This statement concerns the 9% Infrastructure Bond 2026/2032 issued by EverYield AG (ISIN DE000A4EVPH1, German Securities Identification Number – WKN A4EVPH).
